title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance + ADRs
author: Asha Patel
summary: Consolidated engineering standards and ADR summaries covering API design, coding conventions, infrastructure and IaC guidance, model-serving practices, observability, and performance SLOs. This doc acts as the canonical on-ramps for new services and ADRs that affect cross-cutting runtime behavior.
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's cross-cutting architecture and engineering standards. It is intended for service owners, platform engineers, and engineers onboarding new features that impact the serving runtime, APIs, infra, observability, or performance characteristics. The doc includes:
- API standards and versioning strategy
- Coding and repository standards
- Infrastructure and IaC requirements
- Model-serving operational standards
- Observability and alerting requirements
- Performance targets and benchmarking guidance
- Key ADRs and decision summaries

1) API Standards

Purpose: Ensure consistent, resilient, and evolvable service interfaces across Redwood's public and internal APIs.

Key conventions:
- HTTP/REST over JSON is preferred for external/partner-facing services; internal microservices may use gRPC for high-throughput ML telemetry.
- Base path and versioning: /v{major}/{resource}. Always include major version in the URL. Semantic versioning applies to API compatibility (breaking changes require a major bump).
- Contract-first design: Define OpenAPI 3.1 specification in the api/ directory of the repository and publish to the API registry before implementation.
- Field names: use snake_case for JSON payloads in internal APIs; camelCase allowed in public SDKs where SDKs perform mapping.
- Pagination: use cursor-based pagination for list endpoints. Response envelope must include next_cursor and has_more.
- Idempotency: write endpoints that may be retried (for example, job creation) must accept an Idempotency-Key header and return 409 for conflicting duplicate non-idempotent operations.
- Error model: follow the standard error envelope: {"code": "string", "message": "string", "details": [...]} Use HTTP status codes per RFC. Provide machine-readable retryable field where applicable.
- Backwards compatibility: Additive changes are allowed; removals or renames are breaking. Feature flags or API preview headers should be used for opt-in behaviors.
- Rate limiting: per-customer tier quotas and per-route limits enforced at the API gateway. Document limits in the OpenAPI x-rate-limits extension.

API security:
- All external endpoints require TLS 1.2+. Internal networks should enforce mTLS where supported.
- Authentication: OAuth2 bearer tokens for user-facing APIs; service-to-service uses short-lived mTLS or signed tokens via the internal auth service.
- Sensitive inputs: PII or customer content must be explicitly annotated in the OpenAPI spec (x-sensitive: true) and routed to services with appropriate data handling controls.

2) Coding Standards and Repository Structure

Goal: Maintainable, testable, and reviewable code across services.

Repository layout conventions:
- Monorepo for platform components and small infra services; separate repos for large OS projects and model artifacts. Each service repo MUST include: README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, api/ (OpenAPI), infra/ (terraform module), ci/ (pipelines), tests/ (unit + integration), and ops/ (runbooks).

Style and practices:
- Language-specific style guides live in eng-developer-experience/sdk-guides. Enforce via linters and formatters (pre-commit hooks).
- Tests: target >= 80% unit coverage for platform libraries; service-level coverage target >= 65%. Integration tests are required for any code that touches runtime kernels or quantized model loading paths.
- PR process: all changes require a PR with at least one reviewer from the owning team and one platform reviewer for infra/runtime-impacting changes. Use CHANGELOG.md to summarize notable behavioral changes.
- Feature flags: use the standard feature flag library and central registry. No long-lived flags without an associated cleanup ticket.

CI/CD gates:
- CI must run unit tests, linters, and a subset of integration tests.
- CD: deploy to staging via canary for all runtime-facing services. Canary policy defaults: 5% traffic for 15 minutes, automated health checks; escalate if failures occur.

3) Infrastructure and IaC Standards

Principles: reproducible, modular, least-privilege, and observable.

Terraform/IaC:
- Use modular terraform modules stored in eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/registry. Modules must be documented and reviewed.
- State: remote state in locked, encrypted S3 buckets and DynamoDB locks (for AWS). Backups retained per recovery policy.
- Naming and tagging: all cloud resources MUST include tags: {owner_team, service, environment, cost_center, sla_tier}. Tag keys are kebab-case.
- Secrets: use KMS/HSM-backed secrets manager (customer keys for Private deployments). No secrets in repo; pre-commit scans will reject commits containing secrets.
- Network: VPCs must follow standard CIDR allocation. Use subnet separation for inference, control plane, and monitoring. Use security groups and least-privilege IAM roles.

Capacity and cost controls:
- All VM/GPU fleet requests require a capacity planning doc and signoff from eng-sre. Autoscaling policies must include maximum caps and cooldown windows.
- Spot/preemptible usage allowed for non-latency-critical workloads with fallback reserved capacity for customer-impacting paths.

4) Model-serving Standards

Goal: Predictable latency, reproducible outputs, safe rollouts, and cost efficiency.

Model packaging and versioning:
- Every model served must have a model manifest (YAML) including model_id, semantic_version, framework, quantization_profile, supported_max_length, and validation_prompts. Model artifacts are stored in the artifact registry with immutable versioned URIs.
- Model pinning: customer routes and Dedicated clusters must pin exact model artifact URIs. Hosted routes may be configured to auto-update within a compatible major version with change notifications.

Runtime configuration:
- Kernel selection: runtime must expose kernel_profile and quantization_profile per model. Changes to default kernel selection require an ADR.
- KV cache policy: default enabled for completion/chat APIs with a TTL of 6 hours; cache should be invalidated on model update or prompt-schema changes.
- Batching: use dynamic batching with max_batch_size determined from perf tests. Default batch windows: 10ms for low-latency routes, 50ms for throughput-first routes.

Rollouts and fallbacks:
- Canary rollout policy for model updates: start with 1% of traffic for 10 minutes, then 10% for 30 minutes, then 50% for 1 hour, then full. All steps gated by quality checks (p95 latency, token error rate, eval prompt pass rate).
- Fallbacks: if the primary model breach occurs (latency or errors), auto-fallback to a compatible variant (e.g., non-quantized or smaller model). Fallback mappings must be pre-declared in the route config.

Safety and quality guardrails:
- Quality monitoring: maintain a set of eval prompt sets for each model family. Continuous evaluation runs after deploy; regressions of >3% in pass rate trigger rollback.
- Toxicity/safety: content filtering pipeline must be applied pre-release for models that will be customer-facing.

5) Observability Standards

Objective: Fast detection and confident triage.

Metrics to emit (minimum):
- request.count (tagged by route, model, customer_tier)
- request.latency_ms (p50/p90/p95/p99)
- token.count per request and per-model token_rate
- error.count (tagged by error_type and retryable)
- queue_depth and batch_size distribution for inference workers
- gpu_utilization and memory_allocated per GPU host
- model.cache.hit_rate and cache.evictions

Tracing and logs:
- Distributed tracing must attach trace ids to all requests crossing services. Sampled traces for 1% of requests and full traces for all requests that exceed p95 latency or produce error >= 500.
- Structured logs in JSON with keys: timestamp, service, env, trace_id, request_id, level, message, meta. Logs should avoid embedding large user content unless flagged as non-sensitive.

Dashboards and alerts:
- Dashboards: per-route latency/cost, per-model perf heatmaps, infra capacity, and SLO status dashboards must exist for each serving cluster.
- Alert rules (examples):
  - SRE-critical: p99 latency > 2s for 5m or error.rate > 1% for 5m -> Pager (pager duty).
  - Platform-warning: sustained GPU_utilization > 90% for 10m -> Slack + ticket.
  - Cost: token_rate increase > 2x baseline for 1h -> Ops channel.
- Alert runbooks: every alert must link to an op runbook in runbooks/ with triage steps, common causes, and escalation path.

6) Performance Standards and Benchmarks

SLOs (example targets):
- Hosted text completion: p95 latency for 512-token generation < 600ms (regional multi-tenant); p99 < 1.5s.
- Dedicated low-latency routes: p95 < 200ms for 256-token scenarios.
- Embeddings: median latency < 30ms for single vector on optimized infra.
- Availability: 99.95% monthly for Dedicated; 99.9% for Hosted API.

Benchmarking guidance:
- Use the centralized benchmarking suite (eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite). Benchmarks must include: cold-start, steady-state, tail-latency, and throughput at target batch sizes.
- Report artifacts: include perf graphs, environment, kernel config, batch histograms, and cost-per-token estimates. Store artifacts in perf-results registry with links in PRs.

Performance tuning knobs:
- Batching window, max_batch_size, prefetch_workers, kernel_profile, quantization_profile. Any change to defaults requires a perf run and signoff for production-impacting services.

7) Decision Records (ADRs) Summary

This section includes brief summaries of critical cross-cutting ADRs. Full ADRs live in the decision-records directory.

ADR-2025-01: Default API Versioning Strategy
- Decision: Mandate major-versioned base paths (/vN/) and OpenAPI-first contracts.
- Rationale: Enables clear compatibility guarantees for customers and simplifies SDK generation.

ADR-2025-06: Runtime Kernel Selection Model
- Decision: Runtime chooses kernel based on model fingerprint and latency profile; platform maintains a kernel compatibility matrix.
- Rationale: Improved perf across heterogenous hardware and models while enabling rapid kernel experimentation.

ADR-2026-02: Quantization Policy
- Decision: Provide two supported quantization profiles (q8_0 for high-accuracy, q4_1 for cost-focused workloads) with documented tradeoffs; allow customer override on Dedicated/Private.
- Rationale: Balances cost and quality while keeping safety margins for hosted defaults.

ADR-2026-08: Canary Rollout Defaults for Models
- Decision: Standardize the canary progression and quality gates described earlier.
- Rationale: Reduce incidents from bad model updates and provide a consistent operator mental model.

8) Onboarding checklist for new services or model routes

- Create OpenAPI spec and publish to registry.
- Add terraform module and ensure tags and IAM are correct.
- Add unit and integration tests; include perf-run checklist for runtime-impacting changes.
- Register metrics and create base dashboards from templates.
- Add runbook and incident playbook.
- Schedule capacity review with eng-sre if requesting GPU resources.

9) Governance and change process

- Standards changes: propose changes via ADRs in the architecture-and-standards decision-records folder. ADRs require two engineering reviewers and one platform or SRE approver.
- Runtime-impacting changes must be flagged in PR titles with [runtime-impact] and include perf/regression test results.
- Annual review: this doc and the standard ADRs are reviewed at least annually by architecture council.

Appendices and references

- Templates: OpenAPI template, terraform module checklist, perf runbook template.
- Tooling: links to benchmarking suite, kernel compatibility matrix, and API registry.
- Contact owners: eng-sre@redwood.example.com, eng-serving-runtime@redwood.example.com, product-api@redwood.example.com.

If you are implementing a change that affects multiple sections of this document (for example, a new model type that requires a new kernel), open an ADR and tag the relevant owners.
